reading.body:
Three open roles in privacy and data protection at AI companies is too small a sample to support any claim about hiring trends.

The pattern in the data is that the demand is legal and compliance-shaped rather than engineering-shaped. Two of the three postings are counsel and program management titles, at Harvey and Figure, and only one, OpenAI's research engineer, sits on the technical side. The locations are Dublin, San Francisco, and San Jose, and all three are marked remote or tied to a major tech hub.

For AI specifically, this matters because privacy work is one of the few functions that scales with regulation rather than with compute. A model can be trained in any jurisdiction, but the obligations attached to the data used to train it and the outputs it produces are set where the company sells. That makes privacy headcount a lagging indicator of where AI firms expect to be scrutinized, not of how much compute they are buying.

What the data does not tell the reader is whether this is a growing category or a rounding error. Three postings, drawn from company career boards and dated across three months, cannot distinguish a deliberate build-out from routine backfill. The source list includes aggregators and federal listings, but none of their postings appear here, so the count reflects only what the tracked company boards happened to carry on the day it was built.
